title: A Shield Around Me: David Flees from Absalom
summary: Headed as a psalm of David from the time he fled from his son Absalom, this prayer begins with enemies multiplying and voices saying God will not rescue him. David answers that the LORD is his shield, his glory, and the one who lifts his head; he cries out and God answers from his holy mountain. Having slept and woken safely, he refuses to fear the thousands against him, calls on God to rise and save, and closes by declaring that salvation belongs to the LORD, with a blessing on God's people.
story: Psalm 3 is the first psalm with a heading and the first prayer of Book 1, which is made up almost entirely of psalms attributed to David. It follows directly on Psalm 2, and the contrast is striking. Psalm 2 showed the LORD's anointed king installed on Zion while the nations raged in vain. Psalm 3 shows that same king, David, driven out of Jerusalem by a rebellion led by his own son. The promise of Psalm 2 doesn't prevent the crisis of Psalm 3; instead, the king has to pray his way through it. Book 1 will be dominated by laments like this one, the prayers of a king who is also a hunted man, and Psalm 3 sets the pattern: trouble described, trust declared, rescue asked for, and praise given in advance.
historical:
The heading connects the psalm to Absalom's revolt, told in 2 Samuel 15 to 18, probably late in David's reign in the tenth century BC. Absalom won the hearts of the men of Israel, had himself proclaimed king in Hebron, and marched on Jerusalem. David fled the city with his household and loyal troops, crossing the Kidron and going up the Mount of Olives weeping, his head covered (2 Samuel 15:30). On the way, Shimei, a man from Saul's family, cursed him and declared that the LORD had handed the kingdom to Absalom (16:5-8), which matches the taunt of verse 2: “God will not deliver him.” David also sent the ark of God back to Jerusalem (15:25), so the holy mountain from which God answers him (verse 4) was the very place he had been forced to leave. The revolt ended in battle and Absalom's death, which David grieved bitterly.

The historical headings in the Psalms are debated. The traditional view takes them as accurate records of the psalms' origins. Many modern scholars think the headings were added later, and Brevard Childs argued that they reflect early scribal interpretation, linking psalms to moments in David's life described in Samuel. A middle position holds that the headings preserve ancient tradition about how the psalms were to be read and prayed, whether or not they record the moment of composition. On any view, the heading invites readers to hear this prayer in the mouth of a king betrayed by his own son.
cultural:
The images of the psalm come from war and royal life. A shield was a soldier's basic defense, and a king's bodyguard surrounded him in battle; to call God a shield around me is to say that God himself is the protection. To lift someone's head was an idiom for restoring honor or releasing from disgrace (compare Genesis 40:13, where it means restoration to office). For a king who had fled his capital with his head covered in shame, the phrase is exact. Striking an enemy on the jaw and breaking his teeth was an image of humiliating defeat, rendering a predator harmless.

The word Selah appears three times (verses 2, 4, and 8). It occurs more than seventy times in the Psalms, and its meaning is uncertain. Suggestions include a pause for reflection, a musical interlude, a signal to lift the voice or the instruments, or a point for the congregation to respond. The Greek translators rendered it with a word that seems to mean an interlude. Whatever it meant in performance, it marks divisions in the psalm.
literary: Psalm 3 is an individual lament, the most common kind of psalm, and it follows the typical pattern: complaint, confession of trust, petition, and praise. After the heading, verses 1 and 2 describe the enemies, with the word many repeated three times in Hebrew (increased, many rise, many say). Verses 3 and 4 answer with But You, O LORD, a turn toward God that is the hinge of the psalm. Verses 5 and 6 describe sleeping and waking in safety. Verse 7 is the petition, “Arise, O LORD”, echoing the cry of Moses when the ark set out in the wilderness (Numbers 10:35). Verse 8 closes with a confession and a blessing that widen the prayer from the king to the people. The word translated deliver in verse 2 and salvation in verse 8 is the same Hebrew root, framing the psalm: the enemies say there is no salvation for him in God; the psalm ends, salvation belongs to the LORD.

outline.t: The LORD, a shield who answers from his holy mountain
Arise, O LORD: salvation belongs to you

doctrines.note: The psalm models prayer in crisis: naming the danger honestly, turning to God, remembering his faithfulness, asking him to act, and ending in praise. David cries aloud and God answers, even when David is far from the sanctuary.

Salvation belongs to the LORD. Rescue is God's work, not something David can secure with armies or strategy. The psalm also extends the blessing to the whole people, showing that the king's rescue is bound up with theirs.
David lies down and sleeps while thousands are set against him. Trust is shown not in denying danger but in resting in God's care in the middle of it.

words.note: Yeshuah, salvation, deliverance, or rescue. It appears in verse 2, where enemies say there is no yeshuah for David in God, and in verse 8, where David declares that yeshuah belongs to the LORD. The name Jesus (Hebrew Yeshua) comes from the same root and means the LORD saves.

Magen, shield, a small round shield carried by infantry. Calling God a shield is a common image in the Psalms (Psalms 18:2, 28:7, 84:11) and goes back to God's word to Abraham in Genesis 15:1. It speaks of personal protection, God standing between his servant and harm.

Kavod, glory, honor, or weight. David calls God my glory, meaning that his honor and dignity come from God, not from his throne or his army. For a king who had lost his capital and much of his people, this was a claim that his true worth could not be taken away.

Selah, a term of uncertain meaning found three times in this psalm and over seventy times in the Psalter. It probably signals a pause, an interlude, or a response in worship. Its placement here after each major section invites the reader to stop and let the words settle.

christ: The psalm's heading places a king, betrayed and driven out by those closest to him, on the Mount of Olives weeping. The Gospels place Jesus on the same hill on the night he was betrayed by one of his own disciples. Judas's end even echoes that of Ahithophel, David's counselor who joined Absalom and later hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23; Matthew 27:5). The New Testament doesn't quote Psalm 3 directly, so these are patterns, not predictions. Some early Christian writers also heard in verse 5, “I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me”, an image of Christ's death and resurrection. What the psalm does show plainly is the shape of Jesus' own trust: the king who faces overwhelming enemies commits himself to God, and God raises him up. And the psalm's last words, salvation belongs to the LORD, are embodied in the one whose very name means the LORD saves.

hard.q: How can David pray for God to strike his enemies when the leader of those enemies was his own son?
hard.a:
The request in verse 7 to strike enemies on the jaw and break their teeth can sound harsh, especially knowing that David later grieved so deeply over Absalom's death that he wished he had died in his place (2 Samuel 18:33). Several things can be said. First, the psalm never names Absalom in its body; it speaks of the many who rise up, and David's prayer is for rescue from the rebellion, not for his son's death. Second, this is a prayer that hands vengeance over to God rather than taking it into his own hands; the psalms that ask God to judge enemies consistently leave the judgment to him. Third, the images are conventional ones for defeating a threat, making a predator harmless rather than describing a desire for suffering.

Christians also read such prayers in light of Jesus' command to love enemies and pray for those who persecute (Matthew 5:44). Many interpreters hold that the psalms' prayers against enemies remain legitimate as cries for justice and protection, even as the New Testament calls believers to seek the good of their enemies. The complexity of David's own story, praying for rescue and then weeping for his son, is part of the psalm's honesty.

questions: David's enemies said, “God will not deliver him.” When have circumstances made it seem that God had abandoned you, and how did you respond?
David lies down and sleeps while surrounded by enemies. What would it look like for you to rest in God's care in a time of anxiety?
The psalm moves from David's personal crisis to a blessing on all God's people. How can your own troubles open your prayers to others?
